en: First Chapter: Victorious is my teacher Somanātha, the Cintāmaṇi; and victorious is the venerable Lord who bears a peacock feather upon his crest, my teacher of instruction.
Upon the tips of the sprouts of the wish-fulfilling tree that are his feet,
the Goddess of Victory finds the delight of a playful self-choice marriage (*svayaṃvara*).
There exists [a place] bathed by the celestial flowers falling from the fingertips of beautiful young women.
The Reality, whose tranquility is undisturbed by the waves of the flute-sound He has begun to play,
surrounded by thousands of cowherd girls whose garments have slipped, fallen, and been tucked up as they dance,
who bestows liberation upon those who bow with hands joined in reverence— the noble Youthful Form in His entirety. 2.
Slow-moving with the flicker of restless side-glances—the sole source of cleverness—his eyes undulating with waves of the nectar of beauty; gazed upon by the sidelong glances of Lakṣmī;
a lover of the maidens on the sandy banks of the Yamunā; the sprout of the descent of Kāma.
We, these [bees], seek to propitiate the sovereignty of sweetness in this youth who is dark-blue,
whose mass of hair sports with peacock-feather ornaments, whose face is immersed in charm, who possesses blossoming fresh youth, and from whom flows the nectar of the resonant sound of his flute.
The light that delights the world as its sole wonder shines within our hearts, worshipped on all sides by the gopīs whose bud-like breasts are full;
His lotus-face is utterly enchanting with the nectar of His most sweet smile.

In my mind, which is greedy to swallow the poisonous bait of sense-objects, there shines for a long time a certain splendor with large eyes, its lovely mass of hair adorned with a crest of peacock feathers. 5.
May the lotus-face of the Lord expand within my mind—
its lotus-eyes closing like buds, its soft cheeks acting as mirrors, and its face overflowing with the nectar of the flute’s melody. 6.

May some indescribable atom of the sweetness of Murāri— whose lovely form is as charming as a youth and whose moon-like face is honored by the sound of his melodious flute— manifest within my speech. 7.
Adorned with the crest-feathers of a rutting peacock,
his lotus-face is charmingly slow with passion,
and he has deceived the corner-glances of the women of Vraja.
May my life, which consists of speech, be victorious! [It is] agitated by the sound of the flute resting upon a lotus-hand as red as a young sprout, and its lotus-feet rival the blooming,
pale-red pāṭalī flowers.
I take refuge in the Lord, whose face is fresh with the blossoming clusters of light from His sweetly smiling lips,

and who is smeared with the saffron-paste from the jar-like breasts of the cowherd girls. With the unbroken lines of His sidelong glances, which are colored by the essence of the flowery arrows of the God of Love—
We take refuge in the Lord who is worshipped at every moment by the beautiful cowherd women—
He whose heart is the abode of charming graces,
and whose wide, rolling eyes are expansive with joy.

May that certain youthful and flickering effulgence of the beautiful young women of Vraja be present—[an effulgence] which is the eternal playground for the splendor of all the worlds. 11. By those two [who are such].

May my mind bear something of the two lotus-feet of Kṛṣṇa, which utterly crush the pride of the rows of lotus-forests, and which are intensely exalted by their boldness in granting fearlessness to those who bow before them. 12.
By her two eyes, which were overflowing with affection, supported by her sovereign power, graceful in every movement, ever-new day by day, increasingly intense at every moment, and shedding tears—
May the youthful Lord of our life prevail within our hearts.

(13) May my mind float upon a flood of bliss—He who wears the cool, youthful form composed of the erotic sentiment, like the surging waves of a sea of sweetness rendered blind with intoxication; He whose moon-like face is graced by a gentle, charming smile. (14)
May the world-enchanting splendor, whose charming nature is tasted through the delightful sounds of his own flute from his guileless lotus-face,
and who sports with his two reddish lotus-feet, dwell within my moist heart.
[15] He whose jeweled anklets are eloquent—
I bow to the feet of the Lord,
whose graceful marks [are seen] upon the paths of Vraja. 16

May the charming jingling of the jeweled anklets of the Lord of the cowherd girls, which is accompanied by the sweet warbling of the throat of the kalahamsa of the Yamunā— the daughter of Kalinda and the attendant of the forest of Lakṣmī’s lotus— flash within my mind.
[17] May He whose vast eyes consist of compassion, red as the rising sun, [be present].

The nectar of His sweet lips plays within my intoxicated mind— that nectar which causes the lotuses of the sages' hearts to tremble with the flute’s melody, and which makes the hair on my body stand erect, swelling with joy at the sight of the jar-like breasts of Kamalā. 18.

Certain ineffable states arise in my mind for that youthful form who has begun to sound the flute— the moon-like sweet face of the young women of Vraja being kissed by his lotus-eye, which is half-closed and agitated with joy. [19] [He whose] yellow garment is held back by hands jingling with tinkling bracelets...
May the Lord, rising from the bed of amorous play— his locks of hair falling in succession, his ornaments of peacock feathers slipping away,
and his restless desire for further dalliance restrained by the arms of his beloved— shine forth within my mind. 20.
With a gentle, slow smile that gradually subsides, soft and flowing,
causing the hairs on one's body to stand out clearly as they spread forth unrestrainedly through the bursting of love;
and with the mutual whispers of the cowherd women’s playful dalliance, which captivate the ears of the listeners—
We worship the false sleep of the Blessed One, whose eyes are closed in play— [a sleep] which,

having cast aside the interior of the breasts of young women adorned with various leaf-patterns, or the interior of the mind of the silent one, is instead drunk from the mouths of the trees of Vṛndāvana.
We behold no other object worthy of worship than Him,
who is the goal to be attained by the prosperous, who is like nectar itself, who is being filled with the sounds of the flute,
and who is the consecrated sovereign among those of sweet form.
When indeed shall I behold the child?
When will that youth, adorned with peacock feathers, bring coolness to our eyes?
The pair [of deities], with their moon-like faces softened by the seal of a smile dripping with honey-nectar,
and by glances of compassionate, variegated side-long looks, possessed the splendor of youth combined with childhood.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, who fills the world with wondrous grace, cool my eyes! When indeed shall I behold those [limbs] of yours, darker than the petals of the blue lotus of the Yamunā?
Are side-glances, dense with waves of compassion, being perceived?
Or when will the playful sounds of the flute—cool as the moon in the matted locks of the enemy of Kandarpa—bestow some indescribable inner joy? (26)
O Lord, the cowherd girls speak of your restless glances, your tender speech, your gait slow with deep charm, your fervent embraces, and your smiles agitated by intoxication. || 27 ||
With a profusion of gentle smiles and eyes exceedingly long, his chest was pressed by the breasts of the women of Vraja;
he bore an infinite, blossoming, dark-blue luster.
May that great glory of yours, the most beautiful in the three worlds, become visible to me.
Bestow your grace upon me with sweet side-glances followed by the resonance of your flute.
When you are gracious, what need have we here for anything else; when you are not gracious, what need have we here for anything else?
With my charming hands joined in supplication, I pray with a voice raised in incessant wretchedness:
O Lord, ocean of mercy, sprinkle me even once with a mere fraction of the compassion of Your sidelong glance. 30
To her whose mass of hair is fit for the arrangement of peacock-feather ornaments, who is to be worshipped by the lotus-eyes of full-breasted women,
and whose orb of a face is intent upon conquering both the moon and the lotus;
Your eye wavers before us in your childhood;
I perceive that your childhood is a marvel to the three worlds, and that this flickering of yours is beyond the reach of verbal dispute.
What shall I do with these eyes, yearning to behold that lotus-face charming with the playful resonance of the flute?
They are filled with the essence of nectar, yet made trivial by the shifting gestures of objects; they possess wide, dancing eyes, and are imbued with the intoxication of youth.
(32) Even more than childhood, they are permeated by the passion of the cowherd.
The words spoken by you roll upon the hearts of those with clear vision.
Furthermore, [the words] of that great ocean of compassion who has descended before us, with the splendor of his moon-like face now serene—
When indeed will that very nectar of the sound of the flute in His divine play become an obstacle to my meditative absorption?
[Through] His glance with its charming and flickering expression.
We are eager to embrace with our restless eyes— the nectar for the eyes— that playful youth who bears an indescribable restlessness within my mind. 35
By this certain enchanting person, through the playful charm of his trembling bimba-like lips and the wealth of his flute-sound moist with joy—
Alas, alas! Alas, alas! My mind is shaken.

(36) O Lord, as long as this new affliction does not arise within me—a fresh fever that shatters all my vital organs and destroys the very joints of my bonds—let the stream of my consciousness be doubled by the moonlight emanating from the moon of your face. (37)
Before my tenth human state, which darkens all perceptions, rises even from the aperture of my sight,
let this abode of the play of beauty come to you.

I hear the tinkling of jeweled anklets from the ocean of compassion, whose moon-like face has its flute resounding with Lakṣmī, whose path ahead is illuminated by playful showers gazed upon by his tremulous eyes,
and whose heart is moistened by the echoes of the flute’s melodies.
O God! O Beloved! O sole kinsman of the world! O Kṛṣṇa! O Fickle One! O unique ocean of compassion!
O Lord! O Lover! O delight to the eyes!
Alas, alas! When indeed will you become the object of my sight?
O Hari, those other days, devoid of the sight of you, are truly wretched.
O protector of the helpless, O sole ocean of compassion!
Alas, alas! How shall I lead [him] away?

Tell me, how is it that another fortunate woman—whose very form is a festival for the mind and eyes with its exceedingly sweet and smiling appearance, and who has the Lord of her heart dwelling within—is long tormented by a most wretched thirst for Kṛṣṇa? Alas! 42
Alas, with these two eyes of mine, my fate is cruelly opposed to embracing that Child whose eyes are as lovely as lotus petals, even though He stands but a short distance away. 43
With an unwearied smile and lips as red as the dawn,
with the enchanting song of his flute doubled by the moisture of joy,
and charming with his large eyes half-closed as they roll about;
When indeed shall I behold your lotus-face with those two lotus-eyes, languid with playfulness, cool with aesthetic flavor,
and dark-blue and reddish-brown?

When will the compassionate Youth, with his wondrous and playful glances, look upon me—me who possess a thick mass of hair and wear a bound ornament of peacock feathers? 45. (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-verse; the translation reflects the portion given.)

My eye seeks out the charmingly attired Murāri, whose eyes are tremulously flickering, whose lovely lower lip is like a bimba fruit, whose smile is sweet and soft, and whose grace is as gentle and noble as Mount Mandara. 46.
I bow to that indescribable one, whose lotus-face is beautiful with playful ornaments of peacock feathers dancing with intoxication, who steals the splendor of dense clouds,
who is languid with the weight of his grace, and who has awakened the world from its dullness through the lofty, clear glances of Lakṣmī.

We seek the overflowing ripeness of sweetness in that form which is to be touched only from afar in the assembly of sages, yet is constantly visible to the eyes of the cowherd women; a body that enchants the three worlds,
which can never be grasped by words, nor even by the rising rays of speech.
I beheld the Lord, whose luster was like that of a slightly blossomed blue lotus,
gazing with restless eyes at his playful lotus-face while directing his flute-melodies into its hollows.
I dissolve in the sweetness of the moon-like face of Mukunda in his childhood—a face caressed by the moon, its rays of lips bathed in the honey of a shy, gentle smile.
I dissolve in that Lord whose lotus-eyes are as fresh and lovely as a lotus delighted by the soft rays of the sun’s multitude of beams;
in him, whose moon-like face is sweetened by the pride of his playful movements victorious in the amorous battles with the young women of Vraja.
I dissolve in the Lord, who is a lake overflowing with the nectar of the sweet, melodious sounds of the most charming flute played upon his lotus-petal-like hands;
in Him, whose jewel-like lips constantly carry the path of gentle smiles filled with the weight of innate rasa.
I dissolve in the Lord, whose chest glistens with the saffron paste from the jar-like breasts of the cowherd girls, who were intoxicated by the battle of Cupid’s arrows.
I dissolve repeatedly in the sweetness of her lotus-face, which eclipses the splendor of the moon with its soft laughter stirred by intoxication.

(53) My eye yearns for the world-enchanting form of that child of Vraja: her body bent low, her dark brows arched, her form swelling upon the sprouts of her unthinned eyelashes; flickering in her impassioned eyes, moist in her tender speech, slightly crimson in the nectar of her lips, and sweetly modulated in the sound of her flute that never falters. (54)
That youthfulness, that lotus-face, that compassion, those playful side-glances,
that beauty, and that splendor of the gentle smile.
Truly, truly, such a one is rare even among the gods—
[he] who has taken a singular vow to pacify the calamities of the world for those people whose hearts are blossoming with trust.
We behold, on every path, the childhood of Murāri, as fresh and moist as a newly sprouted kanda-lotus.
We behold the head adorned with the crescent moon, a body as delightful as emerald pillars, a face sweet with a charming and variegated smile, and two eyes that flicker like those of a child.
With speech as cool as a child's, with a graceful bearing worthy of a rutting elephant, who is this that enters the streets of Mathurā very slowly, one after another?
His feet surpass the forest of lotuses; His hands, adorned by the Goddess of Fortune, are devoted to the delight of the flute;
His arms are the vessel for the longing of deer-eyed women; and His words are a stream of sweetness.
Oh, what is this child, whose face surpasses the power of speech?
This is the splendor known as Barha, highly esteemed as an ornament for his attire; enough with the rest!
His lower lip is blessed by the arrangement of waves of luster from two or three decorative marks upon his face.
With virtues whose splendor is inaccessible to those of small intellect, her face— composed of the very essence of amorous grace— is, oh wonder, painted with a wondrous and most varied radiance!
Her eye alone is the witness that brings forth an indescribable beauty of playfulness even in all other directions.
Alas, oh! What is this? O Mother, how has the threefold world become composed of youths, so far beyond the reach of my hands?
Her hair is thick, her eyebrows are sparse, her speech is soft, and her eyes are large.
"O abode of compassion, protect us— who have repeatedly cried out, 'When shall we experience again Your lower lip so sweet, Your face so charming, and Your conduct so playful?'— our own kinsman. (60)
When indeed will the Lord hear us amidst the soft sounds of his flute?
When indeed, and in what state of calamity?
The ocean of compassion, fragrant with the scent of youth, makes us his object as he gazes upon us with his wide and long eyes. 62
Sweet in the orb of her lips, charming in her gentle smile, cool in the sound of her nectar-like voice, refreshing in the fall of her glance,
vast in her reddish eyes, and renowned in the resonance of her flute.
Shall I gaze upon the youth, dark as a sapphire gem?
It is a certain adolescence of the father of Love, sweeter even than sweetness itself.
Even more fickle than fickleness itself, my mind carries her away; what can we do?
Her expansive chest and her lotus-eyes— || 64 ||
When shall I behold that young storehouse of graceful charms, who is gentle in his soft smile, sweet in his honeyed speech, and tender in his lips like the bimba fruit and the sound of the flute? 65.
Is it Māra himself? Or perhaps the orb of sweet radiance?
Or is it sweetness itself, the nectar for my mind and eyes? Or is it the purity of speech? Or is it the beloved of my very life?
"This child rises up for my eyes to behold.

66 The fortunate ones, who have accumulated a multitude of merits, behold the Primordial Being—His eyes moistened by His gaze upon the earth, His lower lip sweet with the nectar of a manifest smile, and adorned with the plumage of a peacock. 67
This boy, with his tremulous eyes and a face that astonishes the quarters of the sky,
and with an attire adorned with ornaments suited to a cowherd settlement—
By that innocent one, a festival for our eyes was milked forth—
[a form] with forearms swaying, with the playful charm of agitated glances, with a face like a lotus and the orb of the moon accompanied by a moist smile,
with hundreds of tinkling ornaments, and with a crest of peacock feathers.
This child,
the ornament of the assembly of Śiśupāla’s youths, approaches with his cool, tremulous eyes— a cooling elixir for the sight.
Intoxicating my heart with the excellence of her moon-like face, moistened by a gentle smile, she plunges within me.
What is this? It is the sound of a flute fashioned from the path of her lower lip.
It pours forth upon our eyes an indescribable stream of love;
for this is our beloved, difficult to find even in the path of the gods, the deity of the three worlds, and our very life.
This very one, dark as a tamāla tree, has now arrived.
Delightful with the tremulous pupils of his eyes,
his moon-like face radiant with joy, and the very life of his playful flute-playing resonant— [may he protect me]. 72
The limit of fickleness, the singular limit of fickle experience,
the limit of cleverness, the limit of the craftsmanship of the four-faced Brahmā,
the limit of fragrance, and the limit of all wondrous play.
This is the pinnacle of good fortune, the pinnacle of Vraja’s fortune!
She bears a moon-like face doubly cooled by its sweetness,
sprinkling it with streams of nectar flowing from the path of her flute.
Ah, the abode where my words may roam, the fruition of my merits, and the fortune of those who possess me—this [Lord] stands present before my eyes! 74.
Salutations to the one who possesses splendor, the protector of the cows, and the guardian of the worlds.
To the one who reclines upon the slope of Rādhā’s breasts, to the one who reclines upon Śeṣa;
to the one whose beauty is graced by the auspicious saffron from the region of the breasts of the beloved of the cowherd;
to the one who pierces the very root of the movement of the flute-song.
To that splendor, this "Om," salutation, salutation!
With her tender, sprout-like lotus-foot, moving slowly with the soft jingling of anklets—
The playful flute-song, resonating with sweetness, returns to my life;
it is that very song which, like nectar from the playful flute, sprinkles this upturned pair of my ears. 77.
He approaches, a delight to my eyes, his playful side-glances blossoming with joy as they find no other object;
moving with the playful gait of an elephant, he gazes from afar with eyes filled with showers of sidelong glances.
The Lord approaches with his lip, which yields a stream of flute-music reaching the heart;
with his two eyes, which are like the essence of the three worlds, radiant with their ornaments, cooling, and filled with divine play.
With these two wondrous feet, which are a refuge for the refugeless, this very Lord approaches, his flute resonating in harmony.
He is the one who removes the mental anguish of the assembly of great sages;
he is the one who stripped away the garments from the wives of the cowherds.
He is the one who removes the pride of the Lord of the Third World;
he is the one who removes the heat from the lotus of my heart.
He is [the master] both in omniscience and in innocence.
Beholding this universal splendor with one's own eyes, alas,
one attains the state of liberation. 82
This life of mine, named Kṛṣṇa, which nourishes this face-moon of the cool-rayed one— so beautiful with its repeated praises— triple-multiplies the ocean of my thirst for him. 83.
This very lotus-face of Murāri— with its sweet lower lip, which honors the entire assembly of humble devotees with the beauty of its slightly copper-hued eyes— repeatedly kisses my mind. 84.
May your hands be the teachers who instruct the autumnal upraised lotus in the art of grace;
may your feet surpass the first sprouts of the celestial tree;
and may your eyes shatter the pride of the beauty of all worldly comparisons.
Behold this great childhood, an ambrosia for the eyes!
Day by day, gathering ever more embodied modes of divine play, he captivates even the heart of Arundhatī with the beauty of his smiling face.
Spreading a priceless state of being worthy of praise by the eyes of the Unborn One himself, the sovereignty over the slopes of the breasts of the beauties of Vraja unfolds in bliss.
His youth was fully blossomed, adorned with the flickering charm of childhood; his eyes were anointed with passion, and his laughter was an ambrosia bewildered by intoxication.
At every moment he offered enchantment, his mouth playing the flute as if drinking from it out of love.
Victorious is my life, which enchants the three worlds!
Wondrous indeed is this lotus-foot of mine; wondrous indeed is this lotus-eye of mine!
How wonderful is this lotus-face of yours!
How truly wonderful, O Mother, is this marvel again:
that it has adorned the jar-like breasts of the Daughter of the Ocean, who is the sole ornament of the entire world.
I bow to the great emerald at the head of the vine-like necklace of the young women of Vraja.

Lord Kṛṣṇa plays in an indescribable manner; his charming beauty is tinted by fragments of cosmetic paste acquired during the struggle of seizing his beloved’s hair, while sprouts of perspiration play upon the surface of his cheeks as if they were mirrors.
The body of this Lord is sweet, sweet; his face is sweet, sweet;
and this gentle smile, fragrant as honey—oh, it is sweet, sweet, sweet, sweet! (90)
I take refuge in the one who is the abode of the world, who has assumed a human form, whose sole essence is the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa), and who is adorned with a peacock feather. 91
Even now, he has not at any time beheld with his vision a thousand of the well-seeing ones through the mind or the new Upaniṣad;
yet you have long remained within the path of these two eyes.
O Lord, by what grace indeed do You draw near to me? O Keśava, what is this radiance of Your moon-like face,
and what is this attire— something truly beyond the reach of words?
This very sweetness, this charming splendor—more and more, again and again, I bow to that [face] by which the moon was utterly defeated as a rival to the moon of her countenance.
93. The moon was surpassed by the moon of her face.
Having attained Your tenfold state, O Lord, they obtain even greater and supreme glory;
how much more so, then, the manifestation of Your youth! 94
How indeed can your face be compared to a lotus, when it is so richly endowed with the fullness of many arts and the sweetness of speech?
What else shall I say of that which is the singular beloved of the world?

If you wish to hear that which has never been glanced upon by the unprecedented poets of old, listen with focused attention— [that excellence] which shall always be equal to the splendor of your face. (95)
The moon-lamp truly deserves, for a long time and without artifice, the sweetness of the ritual lustration of your moon-like face.
Victorious are your cool smiles, which shatter all other flavors with the flow of the unbroken essence of nirvāṇa, and which are like oceans of nectar overflowing without restraint. 96

Granted that there may be thousands of those who bear the yoke of aesthetic essence (sāra), or granted that there may be those who have taken a vow for the sovereign bliss of the ultimate perfection of loveliness;
we do not dispute with them, nor, O Lord, do we speak what is merely pleasing to you.
Truly, the perfection of loveliness has reached its ultimate limit in you alone:

the cowherd women, their modesty melting away and their hearts restless; the songs of the springtime, overflowing with sweetness; and the burden of their playful charm, which is somehow indescribably sweet.
The blossoming cluster of my words, which scatter sweetness, find their birth fruitful and restless when directed toward you who have become the worthy object [of praise].
The world is the abode; Śrī is the playful woman; the lotus-seated one is her son; and Smara is [the other son]. || 98 ||
Even the lords of the gods serve in successive turns; yet, O Lord, your conduct remains wondrous.
May the god, who is the musk-patch of good fortune for the three worlds and whose playful grace is cherished by the amorous sports of the women of Vraja, be victorious.
He is the giver of love to me and the giver of desire to me;
he is my sensation and my sovereignty;
he is my livelihood and my very life.
And for me, O Lord, there is no other deity;
may our words flourish in sweetness through the majesty of Your glory.
May our anxieties regarding your childhood increase through your playful frolics!
Those nectars of your deeds, which are to be licked by the tongues of the fortunate, [shall remain for us].

Whether they be the mischievous antics of my childhood directed toward Rādhā’s offenses, or those moments when my mind was absorbed in the songs of her flute at her playful lotus-face— let those very same memories flow incessantly within my heart. 101

O Blessed One, if our devotion to You were to become firm through destiny, as You manifest in the form of a divine youth, then liberation would itself wait upon us with folded hands, while the paths of dharma, artha, and kāma would remain in expectation of their proper time.
Victory! Victory! Victory! O God of gods, O God!
O descent of nectar for the ears, mind, and eyes!
Victory, victory, victory, O God of gods, O God whose divine name is the auspiciousness of the three worlds! 103

Salutations to this certain Great Light, the ornament of glorious Gokula, who is far beyond the reach of words, and who is an ocean of the singular essence of sweetness; in whom the states of being of the virtuous shine forth, adorned by an ever-increasing restlessness that manifests clearly through an overwhelming possession by a rain of intense joy. 104

May this *Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta*, composed by Līlāśuka— the ornament upon the feet of Lord Īśāna and the emerging cluster of fame for the girdle of Dāmodara— endure even until the end of a hundred kalpas, O Lord!
May it be for those fortunate ones who practice the good fortune of the path of his melodious and overflowing speech.

Ah, this manifestation of Kṛṣṇa’s words is nectar for our ears— the speech of the God who is ever immersed in the hearts and eyes of submissive, beautiful-eyed women, and who repeatedly pours forth an indescribable rain of ambrosia into the hollows of their ears! 106.

Wherever my eye wanders— toward those wide eyes, doubled in size by grace, and toward the flowing nectar from the sounding flute— may there, in every such place, shine forth only Your own majesty. 107
Thus ends the first chapter of the Śrī Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta.
The second chapter:
The charming body of Murāri, glossy as fresh butter, having drunk milk, and smeared with drops of curd.
May that [Goddess], whose complexion is like a cluster of *tāpiñcha* flowers and who is adorned with a fresh peacock feather, grant our desired wish—she who cuts through the world’s distress.
Seeing her, the multitude of peacocks, ever-thirsty for the Yamunā, plunge into the herd of cows, thinking it to be lightning; and the host of blue-necked [peacocks] longs to behold her.
May that purifying luster of the body of the Subduer of Kāliya protect us— that very same luster which the cowherd girls pluck as a *tamāla* sprout for an ear-ornament.
May the Lord protect those of us who are bathing in the pure waters of the Yamunā.

May Keśava worship us, who was honored by the flower-eyes of the cowherd women—eyes that betrayed their garments with words of entreaty as they begged for them, eyes tremulous with shame, languidly playful, and wherein the five arrows of the God of Love were awakening.
O Mother, there is nothing more improper than this: that you were made to dance before wicked men without hesitation, merely to fill the pot of your belly.
Therefore, O Vāṇī, who are naturally simple and affectionate, this must be forgiven; I shall perform atonement by enumerating the multitude of virtues of Viṣṇu in his cowherd guise.
With the fingertips of his reddish rays, he has opened the apertures that were previously blocked.

I bow to the son of the cowherd Nanda, whose virtuous deeds are centered in Vrindavana; he repeatedly fills his flute with the breath of his mouth, stands with legs crossed, and possesses eyes that spread the luster of a full-blown lotus. 5.
Slowly, slowly filling his flute with sweet sounds,
tending and wandering with a herd of cows in the land of Vṛndāvana—
[him who destroyed the demons who ruined the portions of the Vedas by slaying those headed by Śatakratu].
O tongue, tell me of that slayer of the serpent-like cowherd maidens—
he whose crest of thick, dark peacock feathers is fashioned at the base of his braid, appearing as if encircled by a streak of lightning in his smooth, yellow garment.

I saw in a dream a dark cloud, adorned with young tulasī, whose arms were as deep as emerald jeweled pillars, embracing me; while Kṛṣṇa, having stolen away my heap of garments, had climbed up to a bower on the riverbank.
A certain charming woman, repeatedly asking "What indeed?
with words of entreaty, drew away from Śauri’s hand the garments held there—her gaze flickering with a frown, a bashful smile, modesty, and deep affection. (8)

who is a vessel of compassion, and whose limbs are beautiful.
I bow to the pure son of Vasudeva,
who, possessing great valor, descended into the Yamunā and subdued the serpent that was intoxicated with pride. 91.
May Kṛṣṇa, who is intent on dispelling the suffering of those who oppose the immortality of my devotion, grant me his grace.
May he wear a peacock feather upon his head, a musk tilaka on his beautiful forehead,
very soft palm-leaf ornaments on his two ears, and a pearl upon his nose.

May he who wears yellow garments protect us— he whose necklace rests near the Kaustubha gem in a space filled with the fragrance of Mandāra garlands, and who holds a flute in his hand while joined by the young women of Vraja; [this was said] by Murāri at the time of sporting in the water.
For those deer-eyed women whose garments were stolen,
either their two hands, or their mass of hair, or their closing of the eyes served as their clothing.

For those cowherd women, whose shimmering, exceedingly dark, and tremulous playful side-glances act as fish in the flow of the celestial Ganges— the mass of luster from the beautiful pearls upon their noses—
those lovely dark curls, moving with great impetuosity, also become like fish therein.
May the wearer of yellow garments protect us— he at whose two lotus-feet the bees hum,
and by the sound emitted from the openings of the holes in whose flute-like row of teeth,
the fawn-eyed women instantly had the bonds of their love for their own husbands shattered.

May the Yellow-Robed One protect us— He whose locks of hair are disheveled, whose lower lip, pair of breasts, and navel region quiver, and upon whom horripilation has manifested through the intense onset of passion;
He who arose from the mine of Devakī’s womb and was purchased by the cowherd.

May that certain sweet sapphire— the ornament of the cowherd women, shimmering like a central gem in the charming necklace of the row of cowherds— born from the merit of the virtuous Ānakadundubhi as the price for his own daughter, abide forever in your hearts. 97.
Standing on the seat upon the neck of a child seated thereon, that cowherd boy, having drawn out the milk-pot situated within the mechanism and silenced the sound of the bell,
drinks the milk while placing his joined palms at the edge of his mouth and nodding his head.
May He protect us—He who made the Gopīs, upon His arrival, blow with the breath of their mouths as if from a mouthful of water.
"We have indeed worshipped with sacrifices, we have given wealth to worthy recipients, we have certainly honored our elders, and in another birth we performed penance difficult to practice. (98)

By whom has there arisen in us a devotion toward the enemy of Cāṇūra— who steals away the sins of his devotees, who nourishes the highest good, and who is graced by Śrī— a devotion that is difficult for others to attain and which is hostile toward worldly existence?
When you are pleased, what need have I for further merit?
If you are not well-disposed toward me, what is the use of my virtues?
Whether a suitor is attached or detached, the decorative leaf-patterns of saffron on a bride's forehead are rendered meaningless.

May that Pītāmbara (the Yellow-Robed One) protect us—he who, at the close of night in Gokula, is sung of joyfully by the cowherd girls as they obstruct the moonlight with the mass of luster from their own teeth;
he whose garments flutter with speed as he churns the curds, imitating the tinkling of the bracelets on his hands. 101.
With his left earring resting upon his shoulder, his creeper-like eyebrows slightly raised, his tender lips somewhat pursed, and his eyes cast with a sidelong glance,
he joyfully fills his flute with the sprout-like fingers of his trembling hand.
At the foot of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), I know him to be charming in his triple-bent posture (tribhaṅga), enchanting the entire world.

May Hari—who, at the arena’s descent, was seen as a mountain-like child by the Mallas; as the flower-bowed god of love by other people; as an ordinary cowherd by the gopīs; as the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) in heaven; as the immeasurable cosmic body (Viśvakāya);
as Death enraged by Kaṃsa; and as the form to be meditated upon by yogis with eyes trembling in fear—he who brings joy to the hosts of immortals, protect you all. (102–103)
Reclining upon a jeweled seat, joyfully applying a musk tilaka to the face of Lakṣmī as she sat upon his lap, and touching her breasts with delight,
he worshipped the God of Love with the tender sprouts of their mutual smiles and moonlight-like glances.
May the Lord of the Yadus, the enchantment of the world, surrounded by cowherds and cowherdesses, protect [us].

When the hem of his garment was pulled, his glance—dark as a blue lotus—was cast down in modesty; it was then blended with the luster of his pair of breasts, which were auspicious and possessed a golden radiance.
May that Kṛṣṇa protect us— he who, as a mere child, embraced Rukmiṇī with his face graced by a sidelong smile while she stood with her head bowed, thinking he was a mango sprout;
he who effortlessly held up a certain mountain on the earth with his two arms as if it were something trivial.
Therefore, you are eternally the lifter of Govardhana both in heaven and on earth;
I carry you, the sustainer of the three worlds, upon the tips of my breasts—does that not count for something?
Or rather, O Keśava, what is the use of much speaking? Fame is obtained through meritorious deeds.
"May there be auspiciousness for you during the twilight worship; O bath, salutations to you! O gods and ancestors, I am not capable in the rite of libations—may you forgive me.
Sitting anywhere at all, [I remember] the enemy of Kaṃsa, the ornament of the Yādava clan."
Remembering again and again my sin, I destroy it; I consider that sufficient—what need have I for anything else?
O Gopāla! O ocean of compassion! O Lord of the daughter of the ocean! O slayer of Kaṃsa! O you who reached the further shore of mercy for the lordly elephant! O Mādhava!
O Rāmānuja! O Teacher of the three worlds! O Lotus-eyed One! O Lord of the Gopīs! Protect me; for I know nothing other than You.
[I see] the musk-tilaka upon the surface of Your forehead and the Kaustubha gem upon Your chest.
Wearing a fresh pearl at the tip of his nose, a flute in his palm, a bracelet on his hand,
yellow sandalwood paste upon his entire body, and a string of pearls around his neck— the crest-jewel of cowherds, surrounded by the women of the cowherd community, reigns supreme. (109)
Victorious is the sound of the flute of the Child, which instantly arrests the impetuous flow of the many currents of the Yamunā;
it causes the mountains to tremble, drives the deer into flight, delights the herds of cows,
agitates the cowherds, makes the sages blossom with wonder, expands the seven musical notes, and proclaims the meaning of the syllable Om.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Śrīkṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta*.
The Third Chapter:
There exists that Reality, the source of well-being for all worlds, the breast of practiced Fortune,
which is as if eternally placed before those by whom passion and ignorance have been destroyed.
[He is] praised by Rādhā, who has spread out a carpet of withered *svastaru* flowers from the trees on the peaks of the lordly mountains lifted up by His hands;
[He is] the wonderful sentiment of amorous grace (*vibhrama-adbhuta-rasa*) attained through Rādhā’s worship, a mine of elegance,
whose natural lotus-face smiles beyond the reach of commonality.

I take refuge in that majesty which is consecrated at the crown of the head—childlike, flute-playing, innocent, and sweet; which possesses the heavy pride of sapphire-blue beauty; which extinguishes all worldly possessions; and whose power of movement is insurmountable for even elephants. I worship it.
The supreme light, whose youthful form is embraced by compassion,
who sports incessantly in the minds of the self-controlled, and who delights in the forests along the Yamunā. 3.
May that supreme light, which, though it governs not the three worlds, is yet restrained by the command of the large-eyed one,
expand incessantly and most sweetly throughout my heart from every side. 4.

He whose splendor and beauty are rivals to Kandarpa, who is the kinsman of the rain-clouds, who is devoted to the playful damsels of the Vṛndāvana forest, who is adorned with ornaments in his very attire,
whose lotus-face bears a gentle smile, and whose bimba-like lips are touched by sweetness—

I bow to the youth of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, a forest of fresh blossoming youth. That primordial splendor, which has assumed a human form yet not abandoned its own majesty; which has ascended to a physical body yet remains hidden in its playful charm;
which has touched upon youth yet not effaced its state as a child—this something indescribable gladdens my mind.
May all those various states of being, whose power is so enchanting to the entire world, manifest at will within my heart—the friend of manifold cravings!
Yet, I know of nothing sweeter than the flow of Nanda’s merit-water, which issues from his lotus-face radiant with a smile and the playful sounding of his flute. 7.

When will this heart of mine immerse itself in that splendor which is cherished by the virtuous, whose ears are unrestrained in their play upon the waves of the nectar-like flow of the melodious sound of the flute, and which is a sārasika bird for the lotus-faces of the beautiful women of Vraja? 8.
May [the splendor] of the sole ocean of merit and compassion nourish us, as it repeatedly robs away the great darkness of delusion while expanding within a mind afflicted by craving.
The playful glance of Kṛṣṇa’s compassion;
the lotus feet of the Supreme Radiance, cherished by the crest-jewels of all the Vedas.
In the land of Vraja,
his face— adorned with a noble and soft smile and smeared with the finest fresh cow-dung— is exceedingly honored by many.

When, indeed, shall I behold that indescribable lotus-eyed boy, whose beauty is repeatedly celebrated by the minds of sages with joy ever more intense, and who is tasted by the faces of the young wives of the cowherds, their eyes languid with passion? 11.

When shall we ever be able to drink even once that flood of splendor, blue as the petal of a water-lily, which has been made the mere leavings of the eyes of the women of Vraja, yet remains for both our own flickering eyes? 12
Its youth was celebrated by the songs of celestial nymphs,
its flute-sounds were tenderly resonant,
and it was the very essence of all delightful perfections.
I worship that abode, whose eyes are like lotuses,
which is supported by graceful play,
and which is as it were the primary dwelling of all embodied perfections.
We revere only the Child, who possesses the playful charm of a blossoming dark-blue cloud. I bow to the pair of lotus-feet of Murāri, who has manifested his childhood out of compassion.
O you who are fearful of being crushed by the jasmine garlands upon the heads of the throngs of gods who bow before you!
In that place where the peacock of Śiva—the enemy of Krauñca—dances, its crest-feathers brushing against you;
and where the bull of Dhūrjaṭi exults, smelling the fragrance of the sacrificial smoke.
I worship that youth, in whom the ocean clings while longing for the playful gait of Hari, and who is like a forest of wish-fulfilling trees in Vṛndāvana;
he whose smile is distinguished by the nectar of his reddish lips,
and whose splendor of complexion follows that of the abode of Varuṇa (the ocean).
I take refuge in a certain child, compassionate, whose long eyes are like the petals of a fresh lotus;
whose body is adorned with waves of loveliness.
I worship the young girl, the Fortune of the cowherd clan, whose peacock-feather ornaments are the merit she has acquired, and whose garland of side-glances consists of streams of compassion. 18.
We worship that body of the Lord which possesses the singular flavor of sweetness, which wanders through the streets of Mathurā,
and which rains down showers from the lotus-eyes of the fawn-eyed women of the city. 19
With a face whose corners of the eyes were dilated with agitation, and possessing the graceful charm of a soft, intoxicating smile,
she spoke in a voice that was both deep and exceedingly sweet.
Alas, the son of Nanda shakes my heart—
those lotus-eyed maidens who long for him as their captive with side-glances itching for love,
and whose lotus-faces are the support of gentle smiles.

With joy, we pay homage to the feet of the rogue of the cowherd women—Murāri, who is exceedingly delighted by the occasion of playful embraces filled with side-glances from Līlā; who is the nectar of the sound of his flute shining in the midst of the performance of musical divisions;
and who possesses a charming smile cherished by the gaze of Rādhā.
My mind is immersed in the lotus-face of the Moon, whose sole essence is sweetness;
it has found refuge in the majesty of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow, a shelter that is an adamantine cage for those who seek protection.
O you who have out of compassion assumed the form of a cowherd, what more could we possibly seek?
May she, the ground uniquely beautiful to the three worlds, dwell eternally within my heart.
We believe that this is the vital energy (ojas) which has tasted the delicacy of Rāma and knows the flavor of the expanse of Rādhā’s breasts. 24.
We—these [people]—believe.
Moreover, O Lord, this mind of yours, though playful, was exceedingly fickle during your childhood— such is the report concerning your fame as the source of compassion. 25.
My eyes are eager with longing, wondering when some calf marked with the Śrīvatsa, wandering as a protector of calves, will appear for our festival.
In her moon-like face, sealed with an exceedingly gentle smile— filled with sweetness, delightful to the mind,
and the sole object of longing for the eyes of the three worlds.
We are intensely longing for Your presence in Vraja. 26.

We are intensely longing for You, whose lotus-face is the source of trickling drops of nectar, who plays the flute with playful melody, and who is the battlefield for the swarms of bees that are the side-glances of the women of Vraja. 27.

I behold that visible splendor, beautiful with the gentle movement of His lotus feet, which is nourished by the nectar-like play of the waves of light from His copper-hued, long eyes; it is made vast by the women of Vraja who are filled with the weight of divine pastimes recounted in song; and it is graced by His moon-like face, slightly smiling and adorned with drops of perspiration. 28.
In his hand a flute, upon his naturally delicate form the beauty of childhood,

at his side young girls with playful sidelong glances full of affection, on his head a peacock feather, and upon his sweet lotus-face the seal of innocence— we seek some indescribable, tender-formed, and mischievous light.

Behold this certain slender form of beauty in the bloom of youth, bearing a lotus-face rich in sweetness, with the playful charm of a young bamboo-stem lip; what have you to do with forest deities? 30.
By means of my full store of merit, I shall behold that fresh play of the Ancient Puruṣa, whose peerless and lovely splendor has captivated the lotus-eyes of the cowherd women.
Having prostrated with all eight limbs and with my whole being, I entreat all these hosts of the lords of the gods with this very prayer:
upon the orb of your moon-like face, moist and sweet with a gentle smile—
May there be devotion to me in the accumulation of merit for Nanda.
Among these flows, I consider even that single moment to be countable within a full human lifespan.
Wherein the innate character of the blue youth is savored through some mode of being—
his naturally succulent lower lip and his divine eyes moist with innate compassion.

We worship again and again that splendor which is desirable to the world— the charming lotus-face, moist with a sweet and gentle smile, the abode of the hearts of those who know true flavor, and the delighter of the eyes of the cowherd women. 34
That certain lotus-eyed boy and that dust from the feet of the women of Vraja—
may this pair dwell forever within my heart.
Even while I am bewildered,
let that child— who was spoiled by the pair of breasts of the cowherd women— arise in my mind,
slowly making the sound of his flute heard.
Let him be recognized first by his playful attire.
[He who has reached] the extreme limit, or rather the very groundlessness,
of words, having perfumed the breasts of the cowherd women—

We worship that supreme elixir for the mind, the non-dual sweetness, the Great Light, which is the sole ornament of the world even in other births. 37.1 The following is a list of Sanskrit terms found in the text, along with their translations: * **manasām**: of minds * **rasāyanam**: elixir * **madhura-advaitam**: non-dual sweetness * **upāsmahe**: we worship * **mahaḥ**: the Great Light * **jananāntare**: in another birth * **jagad-eka-maṇḍane**: the sole ornament of the world
May all my senses be restless for Him whose abode is desirable, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who is the nectar for the eyes of the beautiful women of Vraja. 38.

I bow to that indescribable, most venerable radiance, dark as a rain-cloud, who is worshipped by the hosts of sages; who is made beautiful by the lotus-eyes of the cowherd women, which are fixed upon the orbs of their breasts and hips trembling with the weight of passion; and who is once again the ground for the praise of the Vedic scriptures, whose voices are made to bristle with joy. 39.

O Lord Kṛṣṇa, even for those who gaze upon the splendor of the sweetness of Your human form with restless minds, and even for those who mutter, "O God, O Beloved," may they indeed become like that [as You are]. 40
When shall I behold the broad-eyed one, who in the guise of a youth is especially visible to the eyes of slender-waisted maidens,
and who is the dark moon rising from the new ocean of fame attained through Yaśodā? 41

May Prakṛti protect us— she who, in her youthful state, has established her station through virtuous deeds upon the path of offenses committed by those prostrate before her, due to the innate dullness born of the splendor of her own playful charms.
The splendor that is the vessel for the vows made by those of virtuous deeds;
exceedingly enchanting with moist, gentle smiles that mock the intoxicating pride of nectar;
and fit to be licked by the eyes of the young women of Vraja.
May that abode, the inner sanctum of Lakṣmī, delight us.

May that splendor—the auspicious blessing of the breasts of the cowherd girls, which play within our hearts and shower an unceasing nectar of joy upon our eyes through the particular stages of their blossoming smiles—be ours. 43-44.
Worship the chest of the Unconquered One, which is made to appear like coral by the thick liquid red chalk from the slopes of great forest mountains distinguished by their mixture with musk-paste;
and which is smeared with the mud from the rubbing of saffron upon the surface of the large jar-like breasts of the cowherd women.
45 She who, assuming the attire of a cowherd woman, sprinkles the world with her glances that have the playful charm of sprouts reaching to their very roots.

May the perfection of sweetness belonging to the Enemy of Madhu—possessing the form of a child with a soft and charming moon-like face—protect us as he moves through Vraja, his jeweled anklets tinkling. 46.1 From Vraja, where the jeweled anklets tinkle, may that perfection of sweetness protect us.

46.40 [The perfection of sweetness
Worship the lotus-feet of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
which are like a lotus in a fragrant lake, resorted to by Śrī and resonant with the cries of swans. 47

May that Brahman protect us— He who is the refuge for the refugeless, whose lotus-eyes are like autumnal lotuses, who is beautiful in His blue attire through boundless sweetness, and who is surrounded by the young women of Vraja whose lotus-eyes are smiling under the sway of Cupid’s arrows. 48.

May that splendor of the Lord of All protect us—He whose divine body is possessed of manifest luster, abundance of beauty, and fragrance; who has attained the state of youthfulness while still surrounded by the secrets of adolescence; who is instructed in the practice of tending the cattle; and who is charming through His guileless nature.
He is followed by the celestial nymphs as they hang suspended in the sky.

May the youthful Lord of the gods, most delicate in the three worlds, protect us— He whose sidelong glances are ever engaged in the playful charms of the young women of Vraja, and who is the very limit of the divine artistry of the sweetness of the eyes. 50.

May the form of the prince who is the protector of cowherds protect you— his essence known only to the cowherd women, and being drunk in by the minds of self-restrained ascetics with intense devotion from his feet to the crown of his head.

By good fortune, may that splendor— which is dark like the petal of Lakṣmī’s play-lotus and which, with the waves of its tremulous glances of love, is near at hand for the fawn-eyed women of Vṛndāvana distressed by separation— nourish your desires, adorned as it is with the fullness of buds of horripilation. 52.

Victorious is Kumāra, who wears a crest of peacock feathers from the lord of birds upon his head; whose body is anointed with red chalk from the divine mountain; and whose hair is adorned and bathed by a shower of flowers scattered by the celestial maidens. 53.
May the face of the Lord prevail— sweet, gentle, and beautiful with its pure smile, charming with the playfulness of love,
and with eyes rolling as they rest upon the slopes of the breasts of the young women of Vraja. 54

Victorious is that blessed and great lotus-face, with its languid, playful, charming, and affectionate smile; it is perspiring from the amorous torment of the beauties of Vraja; it is youthful, its lips bathed by a smile as pervasive as the crimson moonlight; and its splendor intoxicates the ranks of victorious, deer-eyed women. 55

May the sprouts of horripilation on the Lord’s great chest—those ornaments beheld by the side-glances of Rādhā during their pastimes, possessing a splendor more delicious than the three worlds, and dense with the intense embrace ascended upon the moment of startled awakening when the Son of Nanda was sleeping soundly at the end of play—be ever victorious; they possess the profound glory of universal sovereignty. 56.
Their lips drip nectar from their smiles; they are adorned with the plumage of peacocks in rut;
their lotus-eyes are wide; they are perfumed by the playful women of Vraja;
their lotus-faces are enchanting; and they are moved by the sweet sound of the flute.
Victorious are the latent impressions long cultivated in my mind!
May that innate abundance of the nectar of fresh splendor, adorned with the crest of a peacock’s plume, be triumphant.
By the fortune of the transformation of even a mere drop or a tiny speck [of her essence], the five-arrowed god of love reaches the pinnacle of his good fortune.
With the vast expanse of her wide eyes, her playful charm—more beautiful than the autumn moon—is eclipsed by the luster of her ever-fresh smile; it is merely the restlessness of a child.

May that youthful effulgence be victorious, who, having shaken off all other labors, is repeatedly tasted by the connoisseurs, and who is the support for the weight of the breasts of the intoxicated cowherd women.
Vraja is the site of his camp; there are but a few cowherds as companions; the calf-ropes hang from their shoulders; the cowherd women are the very wives of Kubera.
Whether it be the mountain minerals of the Śṛṅgāra peak or his glorious peacock feathers— O Śiva, Śiva!— they nevertheless designate this [Lord] as the Sovereign of the Three Worlds,
who possesses the ornament of beautiful peacock crests and a dark, enchanting luster.

Who indeed would not yearn for that Great Light— the beloved of the cowherd women, whose body is sprinkled with the singular essence of loveliness, who is the monsoon for the lake of Lakṣmī, whose mind delights in the Dharma drawn forth by his playfulness, and who is a stream of the nectar of divine sport? 61.
With lips as red as the *pāṭala* flower, with tremulous and unsteady eyes, filled with fragrance and a flood of wondrous beauty—
oh, how sweet is the face of Murāri, sealed shut, enchanting the memory of the astonished nectar!
Wake up, wake up, O mind!
Your purpose will be accomplished before long;
experience this very full nirvana standing right here before you.
Redness upon her feet tender with compassion, profuse blackness in the mass of her hair, and a dark luster like collyrium upon her beautiful body— these are the marks of her eyes.
In her childhood, she was a sweet radiance;
with a mass of hair made lovely by garlands and peacock feathers, sprinkled with wild flowers,
and adorned with a variegated tilaka-mark fashioned from the juice of mountain minerals, she was eternally captivating.

I bow to the Supreme Deity, that young maiden whose body is as dark as a young tamāla tree, who consists of the very essence of the beauty of loveliness, and who alone relishes the nectar of the sound of her playful flute.
Her feet are heavy yet soft, her ankles are firm, and her hips are full.

A hero in his lotus-like belly, broad-shouldered with a wide chest, sweet-lipped, charming-faced with large eyes, and possessing a great mass of hair; oh, what a delightful splendor is this in his forest attire! 66.

One should bow to that one who is the sole essence of great bliss— he who, by repeatedly casting away ignorance through his wisdom, repeatedly milks out nectar with the sounds of the flute, and repeatedly licks it up with his very long side-glances.
Wearing a crest of blossoming *barha* feathers, with a face smiling most gracefully, casting playful glances from the corners of his eyes, the source of bliss for those who bow before him,
dark as a fresh rain-cloud, and filled to overflowing with the abundance of his own sweetness—
I bow to the Supreme Lord, whose essence is like that of a youth in the bloom of his prime;
who possesses, as it were, the totality of aesthetic essence in his face and the sweetness and skill of charm in his smile.
O Lord, this fruitfulness of my eyes’ fickleness— which beholds, as it were, the compassion of youth—
If we place our trust in you, even Nirvana is difficult to attain; how much more so, then, the things of this world?
To those two who are worshipped by the gopīs blinded by passion,
who are served by the lord of yogis and the king of bees,
and who possess the splendor of slightly copper-hued lotuses—
O Master, this salutation with folded palms is offered at Your two feet.
With a heart full of longing, [I listen] to the half-spoken words of the beautiful women of Vraja and their sincere, nectar-like speech,
with the tips of my ears moistened by devotion.
We praise the Youth who bestows honor;
may she of the sweet face and languid sidelong glances dwell within my mind.
May that certain youthful maiden, a wave of compassion, who holds a lovely flute in her hand and has learned the art of tending cattle, protect us.
Veiled by young girls, adorned with peacock-feather crests,
and offering flute-songs dear as life itself, these cool cowherd maidens are a refreshing sight for the eyes.
His lips are adorned with a blossoming smile; he repeatedly pours forth the nectar of his cool flute-song; his tremulous eyes are filled with garlands of intoxicating sidelong glances;
and he is embraced by Kamalā, who is dissolved against the expanse of his chest.
May the deity of the world, who has descended to the surface of the earth, protect us!
Worship the wish-fulfilling cow in his lotus-eye,
and that ineffable compassionate one in the lotus of his heart.
In his lotus-feet, he is the sole treasure of the assembly of sages; in his lotus-face, he is the sovereign wealth of the women of Vraja.
Alas! He is the expulsion of all other aesthetic sentiments.
May he who has descended like the empire of Nirvana,
a great treasure-house of guileless sweetness, the presiding deity of the Vraja,
protect us— [he] whose mind sports with the soft sounds of the flute, which is as lovely as the faces of celestial damsels.
In the forest, may that indescribable Light, the bearer of the dark cloud-like hue of youth, who is the object of our compassion,
protect us— He who is closely embraced by the Gopīs, their full breasts pressed against Him in the joy of His beloved songs and attire.
May that supreme splendor protect us, who dwells upon the sandy banks of the Yamunā and is worshipped by the mellows of the gopīs' playful pastimes.

Surrounded on all sides by those women whose eyes are like those of young does, whose heavy hips possess the fullness of languid grace, and who are arranged in rows with the flow of their passion concentrated in their braided hair; || 78 || 79 ||
May the Lord of the Earth of Vraja protect us—he who, diverting his hands with arrows resting in the quivers of Rati’s Lord (Kāmadeva), attains the supreme state that is beyond the reach of words;

he who, on the banks of the Yamunā where the shade of tamāla trees is dense, eats curd-rice placed upon a vessel of lotus leaves as the water flows before him; and who, placing his sweet flute in his left palm, gazes at every moment at his horn by his side and at his cows.

I behold that Child, who eats the curd-rice placed in a vessel of lotus petals upon the bank of the Kālindī, where the shade of the tamāla trees is thick; who places the sweet flute upon the surface of his left hand; and who, with his horn at his hip-side, looks repeatedly toward his cows.
That which was the musk-leaf ornament upon the moon-like face of the gopīs; that which was the blooming blue lotus upon the golden jar-like breasts of Lakṣmī;
and that which was the perfected ointment for yogins in the ritual of attaining the treasure of liberation— [that is Kṛṣṇa].
May that dark splendor named Kṛṣṇa manifest within our hearts—

He who possesses the luster of a blooming blue lotus, whose face is like the moon, who is fond of the peacock-feather ornament, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, who wears the noble Kaustubha gem and yellow silk garments, and who is truly beautiful.

I worship Govinda, whose body is honored by the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, who is surrounded by hosts of cows and cowherds, who is devoted to the sound of his melodious flute, and whose limbs are adorned with divine ornaments.
(82) In the hollow interior of the lake of whose navel Brahmā acts as a bee, whose chest is the abode of Lakṣmī’s dalliance, and whose two eyes are the moon and the sun;
May that Keśava protect us— he whose lotus feet give rise to the celestial river that adorns the head of Śambhu, and the remembrance of whose name sweeps away all evil.
May the fish protect you with their lotus-like hands joined in reverence at the soles of the feet of Murāri; may the arrows of Māra protect you in the lake of his navel;
may the necklaces made of sapphires protect you at his heart; and may the bees protect you in the lotus of his face.

At dawn, his hair-tufts adorned with peacock feathers awakened by the sounds of churning curds, he entered the cowherd women's dwelling with silent steps. His side-glances were like those of celestial nymphs. 83.
May the young cowherd protect me— he who quickly extinguishes the lamps with the breezes from his lotus-like mouth and devours fresh butter;
at dawn, I remember him whose sleep is dispelled by the sound of curds being churned.
His lotus-face is beautiful at the conclusion of sleep;

his form is charming and faultless, pleasing to the eyes with its wide-open lotus-eyes; he is a thief of fresh butter; his cheeks are radiant with ear-ornaments of blooming *hallaka* flowers; and he is sought after by the speech of the scriptures. 85.
I worship a certain cowherd whose sprout-like fingers are perfumed by the tresses of a cowherd maiden.
His theft of fresh butter removes the sin of stealing from Hari;
his state as a paramour removes the sin of violating the teacher's bed.

May that Kṛṣṇa purify me— he who committed the murder of Pūtanā, yet engaged in the slaughter of the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, and partook in the assembly for drinking honey-wine while consuming the breast-milk of Pūtanā.
O Māra, flee, flee from my mind!
O sole abode of Mādhava, O lover of Ramā, let him be turned back by chance; for who could endure the violation of his own home? 88.
With his left knee and hand bent and his right lotus-hand placed upon the ground,
he gazes at a piece of fresh butter.
I worship the youthful Kṛṣṇa, whose limbs are adorned with ornaments, who is enchanting with love at the foot of a Mandāra tree,
and who fills the air with the sound of his flute from lips as red as the bimba fruit.
I worship the cowherd, the full moon of Gokula, who dwells in the midst of the cowherds, cowherdesses, and their children, and who runs toward me on his knees. 90. Running on his knees.
At dawn, one should meditate upon the beautiful Gopāla, a child with locks adorned by earrings, even as he holds [the flute] with his two arms. 91.
For a moment, setting aside your bow and arrows,
take a beautiful jeweled flute in your hand, and place a peacock feather upon your head.
O Lord of Sītā, O Rāghava, O Rāmacandra!
This son of a cowherd was resorted to by us as the lord of the ocean of milk and as the protector of cows, with the thought that he would bring us milk. || 92 ||
By this [act], an obstacle was constantly created such that even the milk from our mother’s breast became difficult for us to obtain even once.
If you emerge from my heart,
I shall reckon your manliness as that of the sun rising over those sinking in the ocean of darkness.

Like a boat for those who thirst, like a rain-cloud pouring sweet water, like a treasure-house for those seeking wealth— may Śauri come to grant us well-being, like a skilled physician for those afflicted by long-lasting and severe maladies. 95.
Holding in his hands a smooth bow, a fragrant arrow, a discus, a lotus, a noose, a goad,
a golden flute, and a bamboo staff; reddened by a mass of vermilion,
more beautiful than the god of love himself, with a smiling face, and surrounded by cowherd maidens— Please perform the translation.
I worshipped that Gopāla, the lord of passion, the jewel for the protection of the three worlds.
At twilight in the forest, during the season of blossoming flowers, upon the sandy shore in the moonlight,
[I beheld] him whose limbs attract the three worlds, whose form consists of glances that enchant the courtesans among gods and men.

I worship Kṛṣṇa, the cowherd who brings all under his sway, who is exceedingly handsome and delights in the Rāsa dance with thousands of cowherd girls filled with the nine sentiments and the moods of love;
he who sports at the foot of the Kadamba tree and resides in Vṛndāvana. 97.
I bow to Acyuta, who sits in the lotus posture and sings upon his flute.

At the beginning of the day, one should worship the unborn Govinda, who is pleased, whose complexion is like a dark blue cloud, whose pair of hips and shanks are bound with a network of tinkling bells shimmering with fresh jewels, whose neck-ornament is radiant with large deer-claw-shaped pendants, whose face resembles a full-blown lotus, who has slain Śakaṭa, Mārīca, Pūtanā, and the rest, and who is praised by Indra and the foremost of the immortals. 98.
I bow to Mukunda, who is worshipped by the gods; whose luster resembles a blooming kuruvinda gem; whose eyes are like blue lotuses;
who is surrounded by a multitude of cowherds and cows; who has conquered hosts of enemies; whose smile is like the kunda and mandāra flowers;
whose hair is beautifully adorned with the tips of peacock feathers from the finest of blue-necked birds; and who is radiant.
Worship, worship day after day that Lord Mukunda for the sake of Lakṣmī— he who is adorned with yellow garments,

who has destroyed the host of enemies with the edge of his discus, who is unconquered, who has cast off the burden of the earth, and who is praised by primordial sages such as Nārada for the purpose of determining the ultimate truth.
The minister should meditate upon him, whose limbs are stainless, who possesses incomparable splendor, and who shines with a dark-blue luster.
In the evening, [one should meditate upon] Vāsudeva, the source of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe, the bestower of liberation;
who holds an unbroken bow made of sugarcane, a flower-arrow,
a discus, a lotus, a noose, a goad, and a golden bamboo shaft.
One should meditate upon Hari, who possesses eight arms of solar radiance and is dressed in the playful attire of a cowherd youth, as he asks:
"O crooked one, who strikes the door-panel with his finger? Is it Mādhava, or is it Spring? (101)
"Are you not a Cakrin? Is he not a potter? Is the serpent-king not a bearer of the earth?
Am I not the crusher of the terrible snake? Are you not the Lord of Birds? Is he not Hari?
Is he not the Lord of Monkeys?"—may that wielder of the discus, who was thus defeated by the retorts of the cowherd girl, protect you all.

Having come from the temple of Rādhāmohana, he spoke to Candrāvalī: "O Rādhā, is all well with him here? Hearing those words, Candrāvalī said: "O you whose heart is deluded by the notion that Kaṃsa is safe, where have you seen Kaṃsa?"
"Where is Rādhā?"—may Hari, abashed and smiling with downcast face, protect you.
O Vidura, that same love which is felt for the enemy of Mura when offered by Kuntī,
which is felt for Govardhana’s peak, which is felt for the rice-cake in Yaśodā’s breast-milk,
and that which is felt for the lip of a woman when offered by Śabarī and taken by the son of Bharadvāja— [that very love is yours].
Maintain that same joy even here, which was felt for the works composed by the wives of the sages;
for by the mere remembrance of Kṛṣṇa, one is released from the cage of the multitude of sins.
He comes to naught in a hundred ways,
like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
I perpetually bow down at the lotus feet of that Supreme Person, the teacher of all, by whose grace I, having become his very self, am liberated from the bondage of the body.
Thus ends the third chapter of the *Śrīkṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta*.
Thus ends the Śrī Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta.
